title: Dyspareunia - History and Management (Provoked Vestibulodynia / Vaginismus)
patient_instructions: You are Mia, a 22-year-old university student. You have had pain during sex for the last three months, since you first became sexually active with your current regular partner. The pain is at the entry/beginning of penetration, not deep inside. It feels like burning or stinging right at the opening. It settles when you stop. You have noticed the area is tender even when your partner just touches it. Your last period was two weeks ago; periods are regular and not especially painful. You have no abnormal discharge, no bleeding after sex, no bleeding between periods, and no pain passing urine or opening your bowels. You are not on hormonal contraception; you use condoms. You have never been pregnant and have had no surgery 'down below.' You are up to date with nothing yet (cervical screening starts at 25). You feel embarrassed and worried this will ruin your relationship. You do NOT feel intense fear or dread of intercourse - you want to have sex but it hurts. If asked sensitively, there is no history of sexual violence and your mood is generally okay, though you feel stressed about the problem. IDEAS: 'Maybe there is something physically wrong or an infection.' CONCERNS: the effect on your relationship. EXPECTATIONS: to find out the cause and get help. Affect: shy, relieved by a tactful, non-judgemental approach. You do not consent to a speculum examination today because you anticipate it will hurt.
candidate_instructions: You are a GP. Mia, 22, presents with pain during intercourse for three months. In 8 minutes, take a focused, sensitive history to determine the likely cause, explain your provisional diagnosis with your reasoning, and outline an initial management plan. A screen note states: examination and investigations to date are normal; the patient declines speculum examination due to pain.
examiner_instructions: Look for a sensitive, permission-based sexual history that distinguishes superficial (entry) from deep dyspareunia early. The candidate should screen the differential using the five Ps and exclude not-to-be-missed causes (ectopic pregnancy, PID, cervical pathology, endometriosis) and confirm a negative pregnancy test in a woman of reproductive age. Given entry pain, tenderness on touch, no fear/dread of intercourse and normal examination, the best-fit diagnosis is provoked vestibulodynia (localised provoked vulvodynia), a diagnosis of exclusion; vaginismus (with fear/anxiety and pelvic-floor spasm) is an acceptable alternative and is managed similarly. Management: pelvic-floor physiotherapy (down-training, not Kegels), psychosexual therapy/CBT, topical lignocaine, lubricants, and low-dose TCA if severe. Reward documentation that the speculum exam was declined. Prompt if needed: 'How would you manage her?'

criteria: Obtains consent and takes a sensitive, non-judgemental sexual history
Distinguishes superficial (entry) from deep dyspareunia and characterises the pain (SIQORAA)
Screens the five Ps and asks about pain on touch and fear/anxiety of intercourse
Sensitively screens for intimate partner violence, mood and relationship impact
Reaches provoked vestibulodynia (or vaginismus) as best-fit given entry pain, tenderness on touch and normal examination
Explicitly excludes not-to-be-missed causes (ectopic pregnancy, PID, cervical/endometrial pathology, endometriosis)
Recognises it is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring normal examination and a negative pregnancy test
Offers first-line pelvic-floor physiotherapy (down-training/biofeedback, not Kegels) and psychosexual therapy/CBT
Offers adjuncts - topical lignocaine, lubricants, low-dose TCA if severe
Performs/orders a pregnancy test before hormonal therapy and documents that speculum examination was declined; arranges follow-up
Explains the diagnosis in reassuring lay terms, validates distress and checks understanding

red_flags: Deep dyspareunia with a positive pregnancy test - exclude ectopic pregnancy (a not-to-be-missed cause)
Fever, abnormal discharge, cervical motion tenderness or adnexal tenderness suggesting pelvic inflammatory disease
Postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding - exclude cervical cancer
Cyclical dysmenorrhoea with dyschezia/dysuria suggesting endometriosis
Any focal vulval lesion - always biopsy to exclude VIN, Paget's disease or squamous cell carcinoma
australian_guidelines: RANZCOG/ESHRE: laparoscopy is no longer mandatory to diagnose endometriosis; a clinical diagnosis supported by transvaginal ultrasound allows empirical medical therapy (analgesia plus hormonal therapy) before considering laparoscopy

ISSVD 2015 terminology: localised entry pain provoked by touch/penetration is best termed provoked vestibulodynia; first-line therapy is topical local anaesthetic, pelvic-floor physiotherapy and psychosexual therapy

eTG (Vulvodynia and vestibulodynia) / Jean Hailes for Women's Health: pelvic-floor physiotherapy and psychological therapy are core; topical lignocaine and low-dose amitriptyline are off-label adjuncts
Perform a beta-hCG/urine pregnancy test in any woman of reproductive age before commencing hormonal therapy, and document that a declined/not-tolerated speculum examination was deferred
learning_objectives: Take a sensitive sexual and gynaecological history and differentiate superficial from deep dyspareunia
Use the five Ps to screen and exclude not-to-be-missed causes of pelvic pain
Distinguish provoked vestibulodynia from vaginismus and understand both are managed similarly
Formulate an evidence-based, multidisciplinary management plan with appropriate documentation
key_points: Provoked vestibulodynia and vaginismus commonly coexist and are hard to separate without targeted questions about fear/anxiety
Pelvic-floor physiotherapy (down-training/desensitisation, NOT Kegels) is often the single most useful intervention
Always confirm normal examination and a negative pregnancy test before labelling pain as vulvodynia
Document consent and any declined intimate examination for medicolegal reasons

citations.claim: Deep dyspareunia points to internal pelvic pathology - endometriosis, adnexal masses, PID and neoplasia are key differentials.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2553

citations.claim: Vulvodynia is a recognised chronic vulvar pain diagnosis of exclusion; any focal vulval lesion warrants biopsy.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2645

citations.claim: Management of female sexual pain includes mindfulness, relationship counselling, CBT, sensate-focus exercises and sexual-therapist input.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2803

citations.claim: Superficial dyspareunia and dysuria with vulvovaginal erythema and curd-like discharge indicate candidiasis, a common cause of superficial pain.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2617
